draft.title: Trade under the Mongols
card: The Silk Roads were a network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia and lands further west, as far as Europe. Merchants carried goods such as silk and spices along them.
Mongol rulers controlled much of the land the Silk Roads crossed. Their soldiers patrolled the routes, so travellers faced less danger from bandits and warring states.
Safer routes meant more trade. Merchants moved goods such as silk and spices between China and Europe, and ideas travelled with them.
With safer roads, goods, ideas and people moved between China and Europe. One traveller was Marco Polo, a merchant from Venice, whose later account of his journeys told many Europeans about China.
draft.remember: Mongol rule made the Silk Roads safer, so trade, ideas and travellers moved more freely between China and Europe.

a.q: Why did more goods and travellers use the Silk Roads under Mongol rule?
opts: Mongol soldiers patrolled the routes, so they were safer
Merchants no longer needed to carry goods to Europe
The Mongols gave free silk to every traveller
The Mongols closed the routes to all outside traders
a.why: Mongol control of the land meant soldiers patrolled the routes. Travellers faced less danger from bandits and warring states, so more goods and people moved between China and Europe.
a.clue: Think about who watched over the routes.

b.q: Marco Polo, a merchant from Venice, travelled to China in the 1200s. What helped travellers like him on the Silk Roads?
opts: Mongol rule made the routes safer from bandits
Mongol rulers paid for his journey from Venice
The Silk Roads were shorter after the Mongols arrived
Mongol rulers banned all other merchants from the roads
b.why: Mongol rule made the Silk Roads safer, so travellers like Marco Polo could move between Europe and China more freely. Nothing on the card says the routes became shorter or that rulers paid for journeys.
b.clue: Think about what made the routes safer.

a.best: Mongol soldiers patrolled the routes, so they were safer

b.best: Mongol rule made the routes safer from bandits

proposal.title: Trade under Mongol rule
card: The Silk Roads were a network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia and lands further west, as far as Europe. Merchants carried goods such as silk and spices along them.

Before Mongol rule, the routes crossed many kingdoms that often fought each other, and bandits attacked merchants. Once the Mongols ruled most of this land, one empire kept order along the routes and punished robbers.
Safer routes meant more trade. More goods moved between China and Europe, and ideas, skills and beliefs travelled with the merchants.
People travelled more freely too. Marco Polo, a merchant from Venice, journeyed to China in the 1270s. His later account of his travels told many Europeans about China.
proposal.remember: One empire keeping order made the Silk Roads safer, so more goods, ideas and people crossed them.

a.q: Why did more goods and travellers use the Silk Roads under Mongol rule?
opts: One empire kept order, so the routes were safer
The Mongols built the first routes linking China and Europe
Merchants could skip Central Asia on a shorter route
Bandits and warring kingdoms now controlled the routes
a.why: The Mongols ruled most of the land the routes crossed, so one empire kept order and punished robbers. The Mongols did not build the routes: the Silk Roads already existed and carried trade before Mongol rule.
a.clue: Think about what changed once one empire ruled the land.

b.q: In the 1280s, a merchant carries silk from China towards Europe. Why is his trip less risky than it was a century earlier?
opts: Mongol rule kept order across most of the route
Many small kingdoms along the route were now at war
Silk was no longer worth stealing from merchants
The route no longer passed through Central Asia
b.why: By the 1280s the Mongols ruled most of the land the routes crossed, and one empire kept order and punished robbers. Warring kingdoms describe the danger before Mongol rule, which is what made the routes risky, not safer.
b.clue: Who controlled the lands the route crossed?

version.title: Trade under Mongol rule
card: The Silk Roads were a network of trade routes, used for centuries before the Mongols, linking China with lands further west as far as Europe. Merchants carried goods such as silk, spices and porcelain along them.
By the late 1200s the Mongol Empire had split into separate khanates, each ruled by a Mongol khan. The khanates sometimes fought each other.

Even so, Mongol rulers controlled most of the land the routes crossed and kept order along them. Travellers faced less danger from bandits, so more merchants made the journey, and ideas moved with the goods.
Marco Polo, a merchant from Venice, travelled to China in the 1270s and stayed for many years. The book about his journeys told many Europeans about China.
version.remember: Mongol rulers kept order along most of the Silk Roads, so goods, ideas and travellers moved more freely.

a.q: Why did more merchants travel the Silk Roads under Mongol rule?
opts: Mongol rulers kept order along most of the routes
Mongol rulers paid merchants to carry goods west
Mongol rulers let only Mongol merchants use them
Mongol rulers built the routes for the first time
a.why: Mongol rulers controlled most of the land the routes crossed and kept order along them, so travellers faced less danger from bandits. The routes were not new: merchants had used them for centuries before the Mongols.
a.clue: Think about what made long journeys dangerous before.

b.q: In the 1280s, a merchant named Rashid carried silk west from China. Why was his journey likely safer than a similar trip 100 years earlier?
opts: Mongol rulers kept order on most of his route
One Mongol emperor ruled every land on his route
The Mongol khanates had stopped fighting each other
Bandits had gone from every part of the route
b.why: Mongol rulers controlled most of the land the routes crossed and kept order along them, so there was less danger from bandits. By the 1280s there was no single ruler over it all: the empire had split into khanates, which sometimes fought each other.
b.clue: Think about how much of the trip was under Mongol control.

a.best: Mongol rulers kept order along most of the routes

b.best: Mongol rulers kept order on most of his route

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ("most"), while two wrong options make sweeping claims ("every land", "every part") and the third an absolute one ("had stopped fighting"). A student could pick it by avoiding the absolute claims, without knowing the idea. A wrong option with a similar hedge, such as "Mongol rulers paid most merchants to travel", would remove the cue.
